title: ～みたいな — “～-like / such as ～” (before a noun)
summary: みたいな comes before a noun and means “like ～, ～-like.” It is the casual counterpart of ～のような, and it describes the noun by comparing it to another thing or to an example.

patterns.form: 名詞 ＋ みたいな ＋ 名詞
patterns.gloss: 兄みたいな人 / 夏みたいな天気

patterns.form: 普通形 ＋ みたいな ＋ 名詞
patterns.gloss: 先生みたいな話し方 (a teacher-like way of speaking)

body.p: It is the form of みたいだ that modifies a noun: the だ becomes な. Put it after a noun to say “a ～-like ～.”
Use it to describe people, weather, ways of speaking and so on by comparison: 兄みたいな人になりたいです, 今日は夏みたいな天気だ. It also gives examples; 彼みたいな人 means the same as 彼のような人.
みたいだ ends a sentence, みたいに comes before a verb or adjective, and みたいな comes before a noun. In polite or written style, use のような.

examples.ja: 兄（あに）みたいな人（ひと）になりたいです。
examples.romaji: Ani mitai na hito ni naritai desu.
examples.tr: I want to become a person like my older brother.

examples.ja: 今日（きょう）は夏（なつ）みたいな天気（てんき）だ。
examples.romaji: Kyō wa natsu mitai na tenki da.

examples.ja: 彼（かれ）は先生（せんせい）みたいな話（はな）し方（かた）をする。
examples.romaji: Kare wa sensei mitai na hanashikata o suru.
examples.tr: He talks in a teacher-like way.

pitfalls: Before a noun, use みたいな; do not mix it up with みたいだ or みたいに (兄みたいな人).
It attaches directly to a noun. 兄のみたいな人 is wrong.
